turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Hale. Pop your arm out for me and I'll get the observations done before Dr Rahman sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We were ages getting here. Forty minutes from Kirkstall, some lorry had shed its load on the ring road.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): I crawled in behind a bus on Otley Road, so you're not the only one. Blood pressure first. One forty over ninety. No, I misread that. It's one thirty-two over eighty-four.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse seventy-eight. Oxygen sats ninety-eight percent. Temperature thirty-six point six. All very ordinary. Water's on the side. I'll be about if bloods are wanted.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Rahman. Sorry about the wait, the list has got away from me this morning. You're Mark?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Helen, his partner. I booked us in. He'll tell you he's fine.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine.

[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Plenty of people open with that, and it isn't always the end of the story. Where you do answer, Mark, I'll take your word over anyone else's. Helen, tell me what you've been seeing.

[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Terrible sleep, no energy, and he's lost interest in everything. I was going to say six months, but that's wrong. He was made redundant from the depot in February, and it's June now, so nearer four months.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Two.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two months, is that what you mean?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No. Four months, from the redundancy. He always knocks a bit off.

[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking we'll be here all morning if we litigate the date. Somewhere between two and four months, and I'll leave it at that. Dates aside, Mark, is the sleep actually bad?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Trouble getting off to sleep, waking early, or both?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. Mind won't stop.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Still awake at two, then awake again near five, and shattered all day. He just sits.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is that tiredness there all day, Mark?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): All day.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): The interest Helen mentioned. Football, friends. Has that faded?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Won't put the match on, won't ring his brother, and five-a-side on a Thursday has stopped. He used to love it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Suppose.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll treat that as a yes. Is the mood itself low, or is it just the energy?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit low.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about appetite?
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Awful. Half his dinner goes back in the pan. He's hardly eating, I don't care what he says.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Feels normal to you, the eating?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It isn't. I wash the plates.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you two contradict each other on appetite, and I'm not choosing a winner. You hinted at weight, Helen, but with no number I'm not writing a weight change down.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Next question is a direct one, Mark, and I'm sorry to ask it. Any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that you'd rather not be here?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any plan along those lines?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's never said anything of the sort. I'd have had him here long before now.

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good, that's clear from both of you. Let me think out loud. Poor sleep, low energy, loss of interest and a bit of low mood after the redundancy gives me a working impression of a depressive episode. An adjustment reaction to the job loss is still possible, and I can't rule it out, so this is not a definite diagnosis today.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to your chest. Big breath for me.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no wheeze. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Affect is a bit flat. You're not agitated, and you're not sweaty.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Waterworks bothering you?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing I've known. No operations either. Broke a wrist as a boy, no surgery, it just healed.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No known allergies, no previous surgery. The wrist can stay in the past. What medication do you take now, actually take?
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Omeprazole. Twenty milligrams, no, sorry, the box is ten milligrams, once every morning, for heartburn. He skips mornings. Don't ask me how many, I can't keep count.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sometimes you skip it?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The GP printed a sertraline script once, fifty milligrams, and he never fetched it from the chemist. Never took a single one.

[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then it doesn't belong on his list. A drug never taken isn't a current medicine, and it isn't an allergy either. Omeprazole stays, ten milligrams each morning for heartburn, with missed doses we can't quantify. I am not starting a mood tablet today.

[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you know the thinking, if we medicate later I would use sertraline fifty milligrams once daily. I almost said twenty-five milligrams, which is the wrong figure, a muddle with another drug's starting dose. Fifty is the number, and only if the bloods are acceptable and you still feel like this at review. Not a prescription this afternoon.

[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): A few things worth doing yourself. Get up at the same time whatever the night was like, keep the phone out of the bed, and a short walk on the days you can manage. Helen can prompt you, but it's your job. If thoughts of harming yourself appear, you ring the surgery the same day or you go to A&E, and you don't wait for me.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): I need a minute with the keyboard. Utterly unrelated, did anyone see the test match? Looked filthy weather at Headingley.

[SEG0062] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Had it on mute, and rain stopped play twice. My brother went Saturday, moaned about the wind, then rowed about his new fence on Sunday. His granddaughter's three and she bats at the cat with a plastic bat, and the cat forgives her. We laughed about that the whole drive, nothing to do with Mark.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Didn't watch.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Highlights only, on my end. Beautiful cover drive, then on came the covers. Standard summer.
[SEG0065] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Standard Leeds, weather and traffic both. That's all that was.

[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Back to it, I'd like a full blood count and a thyroid function test. I'll spell out why: tiredness like this is occasionally anaemia and occasionally an underactive thyroid. I don't particularly expect either, but I won't discuss a proper trial of medication in the dark. Alright, Mark?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): OK.
[SEG0068] person_1 (NURSE): I can bleed him once you're finished. Both bottles, today, before you leave. I'll get them labelled.
[SEG0069] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please do, today. Thank you.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): Family history. Depression, thyroid problems, heart trouble?
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0072] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His father had a heart attack at about sixty. I'm sure of that. Depression in the family, I don't know, so I won't guess.
[SEG0073] person_4 (DOCTOR): Father, heart attack, around sixty. Rest unknown. Are you working at the moment, Mark?
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Warehouse supervisor until they made him redundant. He's at home with me now. Hardly drinks, a beer of a Saturday if there's football, and he's never smoked.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.

[SEG0077] person_4 (DOCTOR): Living together, not in work since the redundancy, a weekend beer at most, never a smoker. I want you back in three weeks, a firm appointment, not a come-back-if. We'll have the bloods and only then decide about sertraline. Reception will give you the card as you leave.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0079] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll see that he turns up.
[SEG0080] person_4 (DOCTOR): You got past I'm fine, Mark. That was worth the visit.
[SEG0081] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks.
[SEG0082] person_1 (NURSE): Whenever you're ready, Mr Hale, we'll do those samples next door.
[SEG0083] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Come on then, love. We'll get it over with.

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Poor sleep was specified as both difficulty getting to sleep and early waking; caregiver added he is still awake at 2 am and awake again near 5 am.
Chest examination finding that the chest was clear is missing.
Cardiac examination finding that heart sounds were normal is missing.
Past history: broke a wrist as a boy, healed without surgery.
Sertraline 50 mg had previously been prescribed once but was never collected from the pharmacy and never taken; it should not be treated as a current medication.
Doctor explicitly stated he was not starting a mood tablet today / not prescribing sertraline this afternoon.
Family history of depression and thyroid problems was unknown rather than negative.
Follow-up was specified as a firm appointment rather than 'come back if needed'.
